passage: The Class 10 board exams were four days away, and the power in Lalremsiami's part of Aizawl kept going off in the evenings. By candlelight she opened her science guide and instead started a list in her head: what if the paper was long, what if she blanked on chemical equations, what if she scored less than her cousin, what if the result ruined her chances of the science stream. An hour passed. She had read half a page. When Shalini called to ask how revision was going, Lalremsiami said, "I've been thinking about the exam all evening." It sounded almost like studying. But when she put the phone down, the guide was still open at the same page, and the candle had burned halfway down.

qa.a: Half a page.

passage: In their flat in Tolichowki, Rehana sat at her desk with the physics textbook open and her head full of the future. If she did badly in the pre-board, she wouldn't get into the good junior college. Then no engineering seat. Then Abbu's disappointment, and the neighbours asking. Every time she tried to start a numerical, another what-if arrived. By nine she had solved one problem. Her younger sister Zainab came in with chai. "You've been studying so hard," Zainab said admiringly. "I've been worrying so hard," Rehana corrected, half laughing, half near tears. "It feels like the same thing. It isn't." Zainab set down the chai and looked at the single solved problem. "Want me to time you for fifteen minutes? Just one chapter."

qa.q: How many problems had Rehana solved by nine?
qa.a: One problem.

qa.q: What does Rehana mean by "It feels like the same thing. It isn't"?
qa.a: She realises that worrying about the future feels as heavy and responsible as studying, but it has taken the place of actually doing problems.

qa.q: Which choice offered by Zainab could help Rehana start?
qa.a: A timed fifteen-minute session on one chapter, which shrinks the task and gives her mind something to do instead of worrying.

qa.q: How does Zainab see her sister's evening at first, and what changes?
qa.a: Zainab first thinks Rehana has been studying hard, then sees the single solved problem and offers practical help.

grounding: A teenager's worry about exams and her future replaces study, and her sister offers a short timed start.

passage:
The week before my Class 11 chemistry unit test, I barely studied. That sounds lazy, but it didn't feel lazy. It felt like the opposite. I'm Deepika, and every evening I'd sit at the study table with the textbook open while my mind ran ahead: what if they ask the numericals I can't do? What if I blank on the periodic table? What if I get a low mark and Papa has to sign it? I thought, if I imagine every bad thing, at least I'm being careful.
By Thursday I'd done one page. My friend Farida came over and saw my notebook: a whole page of what-ifs, no equations. She didn't laugh. She just said, "Pick one what-if and study that." So we did numericals together for an hour. It was the first real hour all week.

qa.q: What did Farida see in Deepika's notebook?
qa.a: A whole page of what-ifs, no equations.

qa.q: Why did the constant what-ifs feel responsible rather than lazy to Deepika?
qa.a: Deepika believed that imagining every bad outcome was a way of being careful, so worrying felt like preparing even though almost no studying happened.

qa.q: What could Deepika try the next time the what-ifs start?
qa.a: Turn the biggest what-if into a task, like doing the numericals, and give it one focused hour, just as Farida suggested 👍

qa.q: What was it like for Farida to find a page of worries instead of equations?
qa.a: Farida could see a friend who was stuck rather than lazy, so instead of teasing, Farida offered a simple way in and studied alongside.

grounding: A teenager imagines every way a test could go wrong, which feels like being responsible but takes the place of studying until a friend helps turn one worry into work.

passage:
Tuition centre notes, Chetan sir, Class 12 physics batch, 3 February
Saurabh stayed back again today. He's bright and he works hard in class, but his practice sheets come back half empty. When I asked, it poured out: "Sir, what if the paper is lengthy? What if I get a bad centre? What if I don't clear the entrance and waste my parents' money?" He said he lies awake making lists of disasters and feels guilty if he stops, as if not worrying would be careless.
I told him his worry was doing a planner's job without actually planning. We took his biggest fear, a lengthy paper, and turned it into one action: a timed mock every Sunday. He wrote it in his diary. Next week I'll go through the first mock with him and see whether the sheets start to fill up.

qa.q: What action did Chetan and Saurabh turn the fear of a lengthy paper into?
qa.a: A timed mock every Sunday.

qa.q: Why does Saurabh feel guilty if he stops worrying?
qa.a: He feels that not worrying would be careless, as if the disaster lists are how he shows he takes the exam and his parents' money seriously.

qa.q: Why is a timed mock a better answer to Saurabh's fear than another list of disasters?
qa.a: It practises the very thing he fears, working against the clock, so it builds skill and confidence instead of only raising alarms.

qa.q: How might Saurabh's parents read his half-empty sheets if they didn't know about the worry?
qa.a: They might think he wasn't trying, when he was spending his energy on fear; knowing the truth could help them support him rather than scold.

grounding: A teenager lists every way an exam could go wrong and barely practises, because worrying feels responsible, until a teacher helps turn one fear into an action.

passage: Last year, before my Class 10 boards, I barely studied for three weeks. Not because I didn't care. Because I cared too much. I'd sit down and my brain would say: what if the paper's hard, what if I blank out, what if I disappoint my parents, what if I don't get a seat. I felt like a good student for worrying. Like I was taking it seriously. My friend Chinmay studied at my house one evening. He did two chapters. I did a mind map of everything that could go wrong. He looked at it and said, "Ira, this is a map of your fear, not the syllabus." I was annoyed. But he was right. The next day I started with a timer, twenty minutes per topic, worries written in a separate notebook for later. I still worried. But at least I was also studying.

qa.q: How many chapters did Chinmay do that evening?
qa.a: Two chapters.

qa.q: Why did worrying make Ira feel like a good student?
qa.a: Ira felt anxious but also responsible, as if worrying meant taking the exam seriously, even though it replaced studying.

qa.q: What change helped Ira start studying?
qa.a: A twenty-minute timer per topic and a separate notebook for worries let Ira study while parking the fears for later.

qa.q: How might Chinmay have felt seeing Ira's mind map?
qa.a: Chinmay may have felt surprised and concerned, and honest enough to name the problem.

grounding: It shows a teenager who imagines every way an exam could go wrong and barely starts studying, until worry is separated from action.

passage:
Tutor's note, Wednesday

Ankita arrived for the physics session and spent the first twenty minutes listing what could go wrong in the board exam: the paper might be set from the other textbook, she might get the numericals wrong, her pen might leak, she might faint in the hall, she might lose her place in the queue for the college she wants. She said, "I have to think of everything, otherwise I'm being careless."

She had not opened the chapter on current electricity since Saturday.

I did not argue with the list. I asked her to pick the one thing on it she could do something about today. She chose numericals. We did six together; she got four right and was surprised.

I've asked her to bring the list next time, and we'll give it five minutes before we study, not forty. I'll also mention to her parents that she's carrying a lot.

Nilesh, physics tutor

qa.q: How many numericals did Ankita get right?
qa.a: Ankita got four right out of the six.

qa.q: Why does Ankita feel that listing everything that could go wrong is responsible?
qa.a: Ankita feels anxious about the exam and believes thinking of everything protects her from being careless, even though it stops her starting.

qa.q: What countermeasure did Nilesh use, and why might it help?
qa.a: Nilesh asked Ankita to pick one item she could act on today, then practised numericals; doing something real breaks the worry loop and builds confidence.

qa.q: How might Ankita's parents feel when they hear from Nilesh?
qa.a: Ankita's parents may feel concerned and want to understand how much she's carrying, and hopefully ease the pressure at home.

grounding: A tutor sees a teenager listing exam disasters so thoroughly that studying barely starts, and helps her turn one worry into action.

Opened the history book at 7. Closed it at 11. Read two pages.

The rest of the time my brain did this: what if the essay question is on the Mughals and I only revised the Marathas? What if I blank? What if I get less than 80 and Abba gets that quiet look? What if that means no science stream? What if?

In her Bogotá apartment, three days before her university entrance exam, Camila had a list on her laptop. It was titled Things That Could Go Wrong, and it had forty-two items.
Oversleeping. A traffic jam on the Séptima. Forgetting her ID. A question on logarithms. Getting a nosebleed in the hall. Her mind jumping to them one after another, faster than she could type.
Her textbook lay open at the same page it had been on since lunch.
Her friend Sami messaged: "How's revision?" She typed: "Preparing for everything." Then she looked at the list, and then at the page, and felt a cold drop in her stomach. She hadn't prepared for anything. She had only imagined.
Sami wrote back: "Want to do 30 min of logarithms together on video? Just that one."
Camila closed the list. "Yes," she typed.

qa.q: How many items were on Camila's list?
qa.a: The list had forty-two items.

qa.q: What did Camila feel when she compared the list with the textbook page?
qa.a: She felt a cold drop of alarm, realising she had spent the afternoon imagining problems instead of preparing for them.

qa.q: Why is Sami's offer a good next step?
qa.a: Doing thirty minutes of logarithms together turns one worry into action, which is more useful than listing more things that could go wrong.

qa.q: How might Sami feel when Camila says yes?
qa.a: Sami would probably feel glad and supportive, happy to help a friend get started.

grounding: It shows a teenager imagining every way an exam could go wrong and barely studying, where worry feels like responsibility but replaces action.

The hostel study hall at eight p.m. was silent except for pages turning. Pankaj sat at the corner desk with his chemistry notes, but his pen hadn't moved in forty minutes.
In his head: the exam could have questions from the part he didn't understand. He could blank out. His handwriting could be too slow. His rank could drop, and his parents had paid for coaching. If his rank dropped, the college would be worse, the job would be worse...
Vandana didi, the evening warden, noticed his blank page on her round. She crouched beside him. "You've been very still."
"I'm thinking about the exam. All the ways it could go wrong."
"And how much chemistry have you done?"
He looked at the page. "None."
"Worry is pretending to be work," she said gently. "Pick one topic. Just one. I'll check back at nine."
Pankaj opened to equilibrium and, slowly, started writing.

qa.a: His pen hadn't moved in forty minutes.

qa.q: How was Pankaj feeling as he sat at the corner desk?
qa.a: He felt anxious, his mind jumping from one possible failure to the next, all the way to a worse job.

qa.q: What did Vandana didi do well here?
qa.a: She noticed his stillness, named worry as pretending to be work, and gave him one small topic with a check-back at nine, which turned worry into action.

qa.a: She seems to recognise it as worry rather than laziness, and responds with a gentle push instead of a scolding.

Mummy says you're coming home for Lohri, so I'm writing before the bonfire and the relatives.
